title: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope
goal: By the end you can pick the right builder for a job (launch, async, coroutineScope or runBlocking), and split one request into concurrent calls that take as long as the slowest call.

warmup.q: Three quote calls take 300, 120 and 200 ms. You write `val a = async { q1() }; val b = async { q2() }; val c = async { q3() }` and then `listOf(a.await(), b.await(), c.await())`. About how long does it take?
options: About 0 ms, because async returns at once
warmup.why: All three `async` blocks start before the first `await`, so the calls overlap. The awaits then wait for the slowest one. Awaiting each `async` right after starting it would give you the sum instead.

sections.h: `launch` starts a coroutine and hands you a Job
sections.body:
A **coroutine builder** is a plain function that starts a coroutine. You'll use four every day: `launch`, `async`, `coroutineScope` and `runBlocking`. They differ in what they give back and in whether the caller suspends or blocks.

`launch` starts a coroutine and returns a `Job` at once. Use it for work whose result you don't need: write an audit row, publish an event, warm a connection.

```kotlin
val audit: Job = launch { auditLog.write(event) }   // returns at once
val quote = pricing.quote(pair)                     // carries on meanwhile
audit.join()                                        // suspend until the audit is written
```

```java
// Java equivalent: start a virtual thread, keep the handle, join it later
Thread audit = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> auditLog.write(event));   // returns at once
FxQuote quote = pricing.quote(pair);                                    // carries on meanwhile
audit.join();                                                           // block until the audit is written
```

A `Job` is a handle to the coroutine's lifecycle. You can check `isActive` and `isCompleted`, wait with `join()`, or stop it with `cancel()`. It holds no value. If the coroutine throws, the exception does not come back through the `Job`. It goes to the coroutine's parent, which lessons 3 and 6 of this track cover.

`launch` is an extension function on `CoroutineScope`, so you can only call it where a scope exists: inside `runBlocking`, inside `coroutineScope`, or inside another coroutine. That restriction is on purpose. The scope becomes the new coroutine's parent, and the parent is what stops work from leaking.

One detail surprises almost everyone. `launch` does not run its block immediately. It hands the block to the dispatcher and returns. Inside `runBlocking`, which has a single thread, the new coroutine gets to run only when the current coroutine suspends or finishes. So the line after `launch` usually runs first, and the `Job` already reports `isActive = true` for a block that has not started yet.

sections.h: `async` returns a Deferred: start now, await later
sections.body:
`async` is `launch` with a result. It starts a coroutine and returns a `Deferred<T>` at once. A `Deferred` is a `Job` that will also hold a value. `await()` suspends until the value is ready and returns it, or rethrows the exception the coroutine failed with.

What `async` buys you is **concurrent decomposition**: split one job into independent calls, start them all, then collect the answers.

```kotlin
suspend fun allQuotes(pair: String): List<FxQuote> = coroutineScope {
    val pending = providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(pair) } }   // 1. start all three
    pending.awaitAll()                                             // 2. then wait for all
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: blocking calls on virtual threads, started together, joined afterwards
List<FxQuote> allQuotes(String pair) {
    List<CompletableFuture<FxQuote>> pending = providers.stream()
        .map(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> p.quote(pair), vthreads))   // 1. start all three
        .toList();
    return pending.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();              // 2. then wait for all
}
```

Three providers that take 300, 120 and 200 ms answer in about 300 ms this way. One after another they take 620 ms.

The classic mistake is to await too early:

```kotlin
val a = async { northbank.quote(pair) }.await()   // waits 300 ms right here
val b = async { fjord.quote(pair) }.await()       // and only then starts this one
```

```java
// Java equivalent of the same mistake: join right after starting
FxQuote a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> northbank.quote(pair), vthreads).join();  // waits 300 ms here
FxQuote b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fjord.quote(pair), vthreads).join();      // then starts this one
```

This compiles, runs and passes a functional test. It is also completely sequential. Concurrency lives in the gap between starting a `Deferred` and awaiting it, so start everything first and await afterwards.

Prefer `awaitAll()` to `map { it.await() }`. Both return the results in list order. The difference shows up on failure: `awaitAll` fails as soon as any deferred fails, while the `map` version only notices when it reaches the failed one in the list.

Don't use `async` when you don't need the value. An `async` that nobody awaits hides your intent, and in a supervisor scope it also hides the exception. Use `launch`.

sections.h: `runBlocking` belongs at the edges: main and tests
sections.body:
`runBlocking` is the bridge from blocking code into coroutines. It starts a coroutine, **blocks** the current thread until that coroutine and all its children finish, and returns the result. The children run on that same blocked thread, in a small event loop.

Use it at the edges only: `fun main()`, tests, and the rare framework callback that has to be blocking. For tests, `runTest` from kotlinx-coroutines-test is better, because it skips delays (lesson 10 of this track). For `main`, Kotlin also accepts `suspend fun main()`.

Never call `runBlocking` from suspend code. The kotlinx.coroutines docs call it redundant there and warn that it blocks the thread. In a service it does real damage. Suspend code usually runs on a small shared pool, and `runBlocking` holds one of those threads for as long as the inner work takes, which is exactly what suspending was meant to avoid. It also ignores the caller's coroutine context, so the caller's cancellation and timeouts don't reach the work inside.

The Try it runs eight 200 ms lookups on a pool of two threads. With `delay`, all eight overlap and finish in about 200 ms. With `runBlocking { delay(200) }` hidden inside the suspend function, each lookup holds a pool thread for its full 200 ms. Eight lookups on two threads need four rounds.

If you find yourself reaching for `runBlocking` inside suspend code to "just call" another suspend function, you don't need it. Call the function directly. If you need several calls at once, that's `coroutineScope` with `async`.

steps: Read `RunBlockingTrap.kt`. Eight lookups share a pool of two threads.
Run it as is (the good version). Note the time.

code.title: RunBlockingTrap.kt

alt.title: RunBlockingTrapJava.java

try.expect: About 200 ms with `delay` (268 ms here). About 800 ms with `runBlocking` inside (849 ms here): each lookup holds one of the two threads for 200 ms, so the eight lookups run in four rounds of two. The Java twin shows the same cost for `join()` inside a pool task (219 ms vs 817 ms here). Its comment notes a worse outcome: if the lookup needed the same two threads to complete, both would wait forever.

analogy: A deli counter. `launch` is asking a colleague to restock the fridge: you don't wait and you expect nothing back. `async` is taking a numbered ticket: the order starts now, and you swap the ticket (`await`) for your sandwich later. Take three tickets at once and you wait for the slowest sandwich, not all three in a row. `coroutineScope` is the shift manager who won't close the till until every ticket issued during the shift has been served. `runBlocking` is standing at the counter, refusing to move until your order is done, while the queue behind you grows. The analogy breaks on one point: a real deli makes sandwiches in parallel with more staff. Coroutines get their overlap from waiting, so three calls on one thread still overlap, because none of them uses the thread while it waits for the network.
in_your_world: A payment details page in your Quarkus service needs the account (80 ms), the last 20 ledger entries (150 ms) and the risk flags (60 ms). Written as three suspend calls in a row, the page takes about 290 ms. Inside `coroutineScope` with three `async` calls, it takes about 150 ms, and if the ledger call fails, the other two are cancelled rather than left holding Oracle connections. Checkout is the same shape: FX quotes from several liquidity providers, a fraud score and a BIN lookup, all independent. Keep `runBlocking` at the edges. A blocking Kafka poll loop that hands each record to a suspend handler is one of the few places where it belongs.
mistake: The most common builder mistake is awaiting each `async` right after starting it: `val a = async { a() }.await(); val b = async { b() }.await()`. The code looks concurrent and runs sequentially, so the latency is the sum. People write it because they read `async` as "run in the background" rather than "start a child that I will collect later". The fix is to start every `async` first, keep the `Deferred` values, and await them afterwards, preferably with `awaitAll()`. The runner-up mistake is `GlobalScope.async` or `runBlocking` inside suspend code to get a scope. Use `coroutineScope { }` instead.

compare.title: Three quotes at once: CompletableFuture vs async

java.title: QuoteAggregator.java

kotlin.title: QuoteAggregator.kt

compare.note: Both start three calls and collect them in order. In Java, each `supplyAsync` takes a thread from `ioPool` for the whole call, and `join` blocks the caller's thread too. In Kotlin, the three children suspend while they wait, so they need no extra threads, and the caller suspends rather than blocks. Failure handling differs most. If one Java future fails, the others keep running to the end, and nobody cancels them (cancelling a `CompletableFuture` would not interrupt the work anyway). In Kotlin, `coroutineScope` cancels the remaining children as soon as one fails and rethrows the original exception. With virtual threads on JDK 21+, the Java version can block cheaply, but cancelling the siblings still needs structured concurrency, which is a preview API (see "Structured concurrency and scoped values" in the virtual threads track).

worked.title: Make a payment details endpoint concurrent

steps.say: The endpoint makes three calls in a row. They don't depend on each other, so the 290 ms is all waiting.
Open a scope, start all three as children, then await. The function now takes as long as the ledger call, about 150 ms.
A new requirement: risk flags need the account's country. Keep that one dependency inside its own child, so the ledger call still runs alongside both.

Self-check: the ledger call throws at 40 ms. What happens to the other two calls, and when does `details` fail? (The scope cancels the account and risk children, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the ledger exception at about 40 ms. Nothing is left running.)

drill.title: Concurrent decomposition from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `suspend fun scoreAll(ids: List<String>, score: suspend (String) -> Int): Map<String, Int>` that scores every id at the same time and returns when all are done. Then write one line that would make it accidentally sequential.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: `launch` starts a child and returns a `Job`: no result, and failures go to the parent.
`async` starts a child and returns a `Deferred<T>`; `await()` gives the value or rethrows. Start them all first, await afterwards.
Prefer `awaitAll()`: it fails as soon as any deferred fails.
`coroutineScope` suspends until every child finishes, cancels the rest if one fails, and rethrows. It is how a suspend function gets a scope.
`runBlocking` blocks its thread. Use it only in `main` and at blocking edges, never inside suspend code; tests use `runTest`.

options: Either order, it changes from run to run
Only Y; the launched coroutine never runs
quiz.why: `launch` schedules its block on `runBlocking`'s single thread and returns. That thread is still running the outer block, so `Y` prints first. The child runs when the outer block finishes, and `runBlocking` waits for it before returning. Order is deterministic here because there is only one thread.

options: About 0 ms, because async returns at once
quiz.why: Both children start before the first `await`, so the delays overlap and the total is the longer one. 500 ms would be the sequential version. `async` does return at once, but `await` and the scope both wait for the children.

quiz.q:
`fetchA` takes 300 ms and `fetchB` 200 ms. How long does this take?

```kotlin
val a = async { fetchA() }.await()
val b = async { fetchB() }.await()
```
options: About 500 ms: each await finishes before the next async starts
About 300 ms: async runs them in parallel
It does not compile, because await must be called later
quiz.why: Calling `await()` right after `async` waits for that child before the next line runs, so nothing overlaps. Keep the `Deferred` values and await them after starting both.

quiz.q: A suspend handler must publish a `PaymentCaptured` event and write an audit row, at the same time. It needs neither result, but it must not return until both are done. Which fits?
quiz.why: `coroutineScope` with two `launch` children runs them concurrently and returns only when both finish. `GlobalScope` returns at once and leaks the work. `runBlocking` blocks the handler's thread. Two plain calls are correct but sequential.

quiz.q: From the executors track: `CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c)`. `b` fails after 10 ms, while `a` and `c` take one second. When does the `allOf` future complete?
options: As soon as `b` fails, after about 10 ms
When all three have completed, after about one second, exceptionally
After about one second, normally, with `b`'s result left out
Never: `allOf` hangs when one future fails
quiz.why: `allOf` completes when all of its futures complete, and it completes exceptionally if any of them did. It does not cancel `a` and `c` when `b` fails. Compare `coroutineScope` with `awaitAll()`, which fails at 10 ms and cancels the two remaining children.

flashcards.front: What does `launch` return, and where does its exception go?
flashcards.back: A `Job`, with no result. If the coroutine fails, the exception goes to its parent, not to whoever holds the Job.
A `Deferred<T>`: a Job that will hold a value. `await()` suspends until it is ready, then returns it or rethrows the failure.

flashcards.front: `val a = async { f() }.await(); val b = async { g() }.await()`: concurrent or sequential?
flashcards.back: Sequential. Each `await` finishes before the next `async` starts. Start both, then await.
Same results in the same order, but `awaitAll` fails as soon as any deferred fails. The `map` version notices only when it reaches the failed one.
After its block and every child started inside it have finished. If a child fails, it cancels the others and rethrows.
At blocking edges: `main`, tests and blocking framework callbacks. Never inside suspend code, where it holds the thread and ignores the caller's context.

terms.plain: A function that starts a coroutine, such as `launch`, `async`, `runBlocking` or `coroutineScope`.
A handle to a coroutine's lifecycle: check it, join it, cancel it. It holds no value.
A Job that will also hold a result. `await()` returns it or rethrows the failure.
The thing you call `launch` and `async` on. It supplies the parent Job and context for new coroutines.
Splitting one task into independent calls, starting them together, and combining their results.
The queue of coroutines that `runBlocking` runs one at a time on the thread it blocks.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why `allQuotes` with three `async` calls and `awaitAll()` takes 300 ms, while the same code with `.await()` right after each `async` takes 620 ms. Use the words "start" and "wait".
explain_back.answer: `async` starts a child coroutine and returns immediately with a Deferred. If I start all three first, the three network calls are waiting at the same time, and `awaitAll` then waits until the slowest one, 300 ms, has answered. If I call `.await()` right after each `async`, I wait for the first call to finish before I even start the second, so the three waits happen one after another: 300 + 120 + 200 = 620 ms. The overlap only exists between starting a Deferred and awaiting it.

deeper.body:
A `Job` moves through a small set of states. A job created with `start = CoroutineStart.LAZY` begins in **New** and starts only when you call `start()`, `join()` or `await()`. Every other job starts in **Active**. When its block finishes, a job is **Completing** while it waits for its children, then **Completed**. If it is cancelled or fails, it goes through **Cancelling** (children are being cancelled, `finally` blocks run) to **Cancelled**. `isActive`, `isCompleted` and `isCancelled` are views over these states. That is why `launch` reports `isActive = true` before its block has run a single line.

Lazy `async` is a coroutine version of `lazy {}` for suspend work: `val rates = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { loadRates() }` starts nothing until the first `await()`. Be careful with it inside `coroutineScope`: a lazy child that nobody starts keeps the scope waiting forever, because the scope waits for all children, including those in the New state.

The kotlinx.coroutines guide also has a section on "async-style functions", such as `fun quoteAsync() = GlobalScope.async { ... }`, and strongly discourages them. If the caller fails between starting and awaiting, the work keeps running in the background with nobody to collect it. Expose a suspend function instead, and let the caller decide what runs concurrently.
